channel.title: AI & Agents for Security :: FAU Cyber Security Club
channel.description: AI is not a shortcut. It is a force multiplier — and in 2024–2025, it became a genuine competitive advantage in security work. By the end of 2024, LLM agents were solving 95%+ of beginner CTF challenges autonomously. In 2025, one AI system placed first at a live competition and took a $50,000 prize. An autonomous pen-testing AI reached #1 on HackerOne’s US leaderboard. This section covers what AI can actually do, which models to use, how to set them up, and how to build workflows and agents for security work.

item.title: What AI Can Actually Do
item.description: Skip the hype. Here is what AI has demonstrably done in security competitions and research, with numbers. CTF Benchmarks picoCTF-level challenges — effectively solved Palisade Research (Dec 2024): A plain ReAct-based agent with plan-and-solve prompting hit 95% overall on the InterCode-CTF benchmark — 100% on General Skills, Binary Exploitation, and Web Exploitation. Most challenges were solved in 1–2 turns. The benchmark is now considered saturated at this difficulty level.

item.title: Models & When to Use Them
item.description: Different models have different strengths. For security work the relevant axes are: reasoning depth, code quality, context window, cost, and whether you can run it locally. Cloud Models Claude (Anthropic) Claude Sonnet is the best coding and reasoning model for day-to-day work. It handles long context well, is precise about what it does not know, and produces clean code.

item.title: Setting Up Your AI Toolkit
item.description: Three setups worth knowing: Claude Code with ECC for daily security work, a local Ollama stack for offline or sensitive targets, and CAI for automated CTF solving. Claude Code + ECC (Recommended Starting Point) Claude Code is Anthropic’s CLI tool. It reads your project context and runs tools in your terminal — write files, run commands, search code, browse the web.

item.title: Practical Workflows
item.description: These are repeatable patterns — not one-off prompts. Build them into habits and you get compounding results. CTF Workflow with AI The loop that works: 1. Enumerate manually (understand what you have) 2. Ask AI to analyze the enumeration output 3. Generate exploit / script with AI 4. Run it, get output 5. Feed output back to AI for interpretation 6. Iterate AI is most useful at steps 2, 3, and 5. You own steps 1, 4, and the final judgment call.

item.title: Building Agents
item.description: A single AI model answering questions is useful. An agent that can run tools, observe results, and adapt its next action is a different category of useful. The systems that won CTF competitions and topped bug bounty leaderboards were not chat interfaces — they were agents with tool access operating in loops.
